facts.claim: 'The Spark' is the opening track on William Prince's second album Reliever, released February 7, 2020.
All tracks on Reliever, including 'The Spark', were written by William Prince.
'The Spark' was produced by Dave Cobb and recorded at Historic RCA Studio A in Nashville. Brandon Bell engineered and mixed it.

Bandcamp credits for 'The Spark' list William Prince (vocals, acoustic guitar), Dave Cobb (electric and acoustic guitar), Chris Powell (drums, percussion), Adam Gardner (bass, piano, keyboards, strings) and Kristen Robers (background vocals).
'The Spark' was the lead single from Reliever. Its video was directed by Christopher Smets, and Prince said he wanted it to show more warmth than his earlier 'Breathless' video.
Prince said 'The Spark' is about hope in finding someone who lights you up amid darkness. He added that true love can burn so bright when it finds its spark.

Prince says he wrote 'The Spark' early on, and he thought of it as a love song to bring to the Nashville sessions after worrying he had nothing like 'Breathless'. Cobb suggested saving the line 'you're the spark' for the final line.
Reliever's songs took shape while Prince dealt with his father's death, the birth of his son, and a separation from his son's mother. Prince described the record as a testament to resilience.
Prince reunited with producers Dave Cobb (Nashville) and Scott Nolan (Winnipeg), who worked on his Juno-winning debut Earthly Days.

Prince is from Peguis First Nation, north of Winnipeg. He had planned a career as a doctor before turning to music, and his influences include his preacher-musician father, Kris Kristofferson and Charley Pride.

research.lineage: The song sits in Canadian roots/Americana singer-songwriter tradition, shaped by gospel and classic outlaw country and recorded with Nashville producer Dave Cobb.

draft:
The question at the center of **The Spark** isn't "will you stay with me." It's harder than that: "My love if we burn would you burn right next to me?" William Prince doesn't promise safety. He asks for company inside the danger, and that's a braver, more grown-up kind of love song than the title lets on.

The narrator is talking to someone braced for abandonment. "You always think I'm leavin'" is the line that sets the stakes, and the answer is the plainest reassurance there is: *Darling, it'll be ok.* There's tenderness in it, and a little fatigue too, the sound of someone who has said this before and will keep saying it. The chorus turns a cliché into something truer. "All these bridges we cross all have water underneath" admits that every step forward rests on old hurt, the "ashes of lost love" that make it hard to breathe. The fire never gets put out. It gets shared.

The late verse breaks the song's easy rhythm. The lines crowd up, rhyming *met you*, *forget you*, *let you* in quick succession, and the narrator finally owns his side of it: pure intentions, but "a beacon for chaos," carrying a pain he can't take a day off from. Pride and apology sit next to each other there, unresolved. Then comes the payoff Prince held back on Dave Cobb's suggestion: the very last line finally names the beloved as the spark. Waiting that long makes it land like a confession.

The arrangement keeps things warm and close. Fingerpicked acoustic guitar rolls under a walking bass line, the drums keep a simple, steady beat, and steel guitar draws long, sustained lines between Prince's phrases. The tempo is slow and unhurried. His voice is clear and mid-range, smooth and unforced, sitting in a clean mix with just enough room around it. It was cut at Historic RCA Studio A in Nashville with Cobb producing, and it carries that room's polish without losing the front-porch plainness.

Prince, who comes from Peguis First Nation north of Winnipeg, names his preacher-musician father, Kris Kristofferson and Charley Pride as touchstones, and you can hear all three: the gospel faith in rescue, the Kristofferson habit of loving with your flaws in plain view, the country singer's unshowy baritone ease. Reliever took shape around his father's death, his son's birth and a separation. Opening it with a song about hope that doesn't pretend the fire is out feels exactly right.

What sticks is the shape of the promise: not "I'll keep you from burning," but "I'll be standing in it too," and you hear how much steadier that is to lean on.
